nodes.name: Mountain grassland grass
nodes.desc: A perennial bunch grass of African grasslands. Montane grassland like this caps the Nimba ridge above the forest and is home to the endemic Nimba toad.

nodes.name: Guinea plum
nodes.desc: A large evergreen tree that gives its name to the mossy Parinari forests on Nimba. Its fruit is eaten by chimpanzees and other animals.

nodes.name: Wild figs
nodes.desc: Fig trees fruit through the year in many tropical forests and are a food source for bats, birds and primates.

nodes.name: Stream algae
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae film on stones in the clear streams that drain the mountain springs.

nodes.name: Egyptian rousette
nodes.desc: A fruit bat recorded near Nimba in GBIF data. Fruit bats feed on figs and other fruit and spread seeds at night.

nodes.name: Pygmy hippopotamus
nodes.desc: A forest and swamp herbivore of West Africa, mostly in Liberia with small numbers in Guinea. It eats ferns, herbs and fallen fruit, and leopards take its young.

nodes.name: Western chimpanzee
nodes.desc: The Nimba area is known for chimpanzees that use stones as tools. They eat mostly fruit, including that of Guinea plum.

nodes.name: Zebra duiker
nodes.desc: A small forest antelope that eats fruit, leaves and seeds and can crack hard fruit shells. It is a threatened species of the Upper Guinea forests.

nodes.name: African pied hornbill
nodes.desc: A frequently recorded forest bird of the Nimba circle. Hornbills take fruit and insects.

nodes.name: Marginated Congo chafer
nodes.desc: A colourful beetle recorded near Nimba. Adults feed on fruit and flowers and are prey for birds and small mammals.

nodes.name: Typical striped grass mouse
nodes.desc: A small rodent of grassland, forest edge and secondary forest up to about 1,700 m. GloBI records the rhinoceros viper eating it.

nodes.name: Stream insects
nodes.desc: Insect larvae and other small animals that graze algae and debris in the mountain streams.

nodes.name: Nimba viviparous toad
nodes.desc: A critically endangered toad found only in the high grasslands of Nimba at about 1,200 to 1,680 m. It gives birth to live young and does not tolerate disturbed ground.

nodes.name: Nimba otter shrew
nodes.desc: A small nocturnal semi-aquatic insectivore living along creeks in the Nimba area. Mining runoff threatens its streams.

nodes.name: Common kusimanse
nodes.desc: A small social mongoose of West African forest floors that forages for insects and other small animals.

nodes.name: Rhinoceros viper
nodes.desc: A forest viper recorded in the Nimba circle. GloBI records it eating the striped grass mouse.

nodes.name: Leopard
nodes.desc: The top predator of West African forests. Wikipedia lists it among the predators of young pygmy hippos.

nodes.name: Rain and cloud
nodes.desc: The southern slopes are wetter than the northern ones. Mist and cloud feed the mossy forest on the ridge.

nodes.name: Mountain springs
nodes.desc: About fifty springs make Nimba a water tower for the Cavally, Cestos and Sassandra rivers.

nodes.name: Land-clearing fires
nodes.desc: UNESCO lists regular fires set for farming and grazing around the reserve as a threat. Fire also shapes the grassland.

nodes.name: Mountain soils
nodes.desc: Thin ridge soils and the nutrients released from dead leaves feed the forest and grassland.

nodes.name: Dung beetles & fungi
nodes.desc: Large dung beetles such as Heliocopris are among the most recorded insects here. With fungi they recycle dead matter into soil.
